claim: Inhibitory interneurons are believed to realize critical gating functions in cortical circuits.
source: Inhibitory interneurons are believed to realize critical gating functions in cortical circuits, but it has been difficult to ascertain the content of gated information for well-characterized interneurons in primate cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific belief regarding interneuron function.

claim: It has been difficult to ascertain the content of gated information for well-characterized interneurons in primate cortex.
source: Inhibitory interneurons are believed to realize critical gating functions in cortical circuits, but it has been difficult to ascertain the content of gated information for well-characterized interneurons in primate cortex.
evidence: This statement reflects a gap in current knowledge about primate interneurons.

claim: Subclasses of narrow spiking neurons have a relative suppressive effect on the local circuit indicating they are inhibitory interneurons.
source: We find that subclasses of narrow spiking neurons have a relative suppressive effect on the local circuit indicating they are inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered multiunit activity analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: One interneuron subclass showed prominent firing rate modulations and (35–45 Hz) gamma synchronous spiking during periods of uncertainty in both LPFC and ACC.
source: One of these interneuron subclasses showed prominent firing rate modulations and (35–45 Hz) gamma synchronous spiking during periods of uncertainty in both, lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings and analysis.

claim: In LPFC, this interneuron subclass activated when the uncertainty of attention cues was resolved during flexible learning.
source: In LPFC, this interneuron subclass activated when the uncertainty of attention cues was resolved during flexible learning, whereas in ACC it fired and gamma-synchronized when outcomes were uncertain and prediction errors were high during learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates correlated with choice probability.

claim: In ACC, this interneuron subclass fired and gamma-synchronized when outcomes were uncertain and prediction errors were high during learning.
source: In LPFC, this interneuron subclass activated when the uncertainty of attention cues was resolved during flexible learning, whereas in ACC it fired and gamma-synchronized when outcomes were uncertain and prediction errors were high during learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates correlated with reward prediction errors.

claim: Computational modeling of interneuron-specific gamma band activity suggests it could reflect a soft winner-take-all gating of information having high degree of uncertainty.
source: Computational modeling of this interneuron-specific gamma band activity in simple circuit motifs suggests it could reflect a soft winner-take-all gating of information having high degree of uncertainty.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Groups of fast spiking interneurons with basket cell or chandelier morphologies have consistently been found to be abnormal in individuals with schizophrenia.
source: Groups of fast spiking interneurons with basket cell or chandelier morphologies have consistently been found to be abnormal in individuals with schizophrenia and linked to dysfunctional working memory and reduced control of attention (Dienel and Lewis, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Abnormal fast spiking interneurons in schizophrenia are linked to dysfunctional working memory and reduced control of attention.
source: Groups of fast spiking interneurons with basket cell or chandelier morphologies have consistently been found to be abnormal in individuals with schizophrenia and linked to dysfunctional working memory and reduced control of attention (Dienel and Lewis, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Altered functioning of a non-fast spiking interneuron class is linked to reduced GABAergic tone in individuals with severe major depression.
source: Altered functioning of a non-fast spiking interneuron class is linked to reduced GABAergic tone in individuals with severe major depression (Levinson et al., 2010; Fee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The circuit functions of different subtypes of interneurons in prefrontal cortices are important to regulate specific aspects of cognitive and affective functioning.
source: These findings suggest that the circuit functions of different subtypes of interneurons in prefrontal cortices are important to regulate specific aspects of cognitive and affective functioning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about interneuron dysfunction in psychiatric disorders.

claim: Prefrontal CCK expressing basket cells impose inhibition that is required during the choice epoch, but not during the delay epoch of a working memory task.
source: Prefrontal CCK expressing basket cells have been shown to impose inhibition that is required during the choice epoch, but not during the delay epoch of a working memory task (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior rodent literature.

claim: Retention of visual information during working memory delays requires activation specifically of PV+ expressing fast spiking interneurons.
source: In contrast, retention of visual information during working memory delays has been shown to require activation specifically of PV+ expressing fast spiking interneurons (Lagler et al., 2016; Kamigaki and Dan, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rodent literature.

claim: PV+ neurons in prefrontal circuits have been associated with attentional orienting.
source: In the same prefrontal circuits, the PV+ neurons have also been associated with attentional orienting (Kim et al., 2016), shifting of attentional sets and response strategies during reward learning (Cho et al., 2015; Canetta et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2020), and with spatial reward choices (Lagler et al., 2016), among other functions (Pinto and Dan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior rodent literature.

claim: PV+ neurons have been associated with shifting of attentional sets and response strategies during reward learning.
source: In the same prefrontal circuits, the PV+ neurons have also been associated with attentional orienting (Kim et al., 2016), shifting of attentional sets and response strategies during reward learning (Cho et al., 2015; Canetta et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2020), and with spatial reward choices (Lagler et al., 2016), among other functions (Pinto and Dan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rodent literature.

claim: Somatostatin expressing neurons (SOM+) are necessary during the initial encoding phase of a working memory task but not during the delay.
source: Distinct from PV+, the group of somatostatin expressing neurons (SOM+) have been shown to be necessary during the initial encoding phase of a working memory task but not during the delay (Abbas et al., 2018), and in anterior cingulate cortex they activate specifically during the approach of reward sites (Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior rodent literature.

claim: In anterior cingulate cortex, SOM+ neurons activate specifically during the approach of reward sites.
source: Distinct from PV+, the group of somatostatin expressing neurons (SOM+) have been shown to be necessary during the initial encoding phase of a working memory task but not during the delay (Abbas et al., 2018), and in anterior cingulate cortex they activate specifically during the approach of reward sites (Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rodent literature.

claim: Rodent prefrontal cortex interneurons expressing PV, SOM, or CCK fulfill separable, unique roles at different processing stages during goal-directed task performance.
source: Taken together, these findings illustrate that rodent prefrontal cortex interneurons expressing PV, SOM, or CCK fulfill separable, unique roles at different processing stages during goal-directed task performance (Pinto and Dan, 2015; Lagler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple citations to rodent literature.

claim: Most existing knowledge about cell-specific circuit functions in primate prefrontal cortex is indirectly inferred from studies that distinguish only one group of putative interneurons that show narrow action potential spike width.
source: While there are recent advances using optogenetic tools for use in primates (Acker et al., 2016; Dimidschstein et al., 2016; Gong et al., 2020), most existing knowledge about cell-specific circuit functions are indirectly inferred from studies that distinguish only one group of putative interneurons that show narrow action potential spike width.
evidence: This statement characterizes the current state of knowledge in primate research.

claim: Narrow spiking putative interneurons in lateral prefrontal cortex more likely encode categorical information during working memory delays compared to broad spiking neurons.
source: Compared to broad spiking neurons the group of narrow spiking, putative interneurons in lateral prefrontal cortex have been found to more likely encode categorical information during working memory delays (Diester and Nieder, 2008), show stronger stimulus onset responses during cognitive control tasks (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger attentional modulation (Thiele et al., 2016), more location-specific encoding of task rules (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger reduction of firing selectivity for task irrelevant stimulus features (Hussar and Pasternak, 2009), stronger encoding of errors and loss (Shen et al., 2015; Sajad et al., 2019), more likely encoding of outcome history (Kawai et al., 2019), and stronger encoding of feature-specific reward prediction errors (Oemisch et al., 2019), amongst other unique firing characteristics (Constantinidis and Goldman-Rakic, 2002; Ardid et al., 2015; Rich and Wallis, 2017; Voloh and Womelsdorf, 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior primate literature.

claim: Narrow spiking putative interneurons show stronger stimulus onset responses during cognitive control tasks compared to broad spiking neurons.
source: Compared to broad spiking neurons the group of narrow spiking, putative interneurons in lateral prefrontal cortex have been found to more likely encode categorical information during working memory delays (Diester and Nieder, 2008), show stronger stimulus onset responses during cognitive control tasks (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger attentional modulation (Thiele et al., 2016), more location-specific encoding of task rules (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger reduction of firing selectivity for task irrelevant stimulus features (Hussar and Pasternak, 2009), stronger encoding of errors and loss (Shen et al., 2015; Sajad et al., 2019), more likely encoding of outcome history (Kawai et al., 2019), and stronger encoding of feature-specific reward prediction errors (Oemisch et al., 2019), amongst other unique firing characteristics (Constantinidis and Goldman-Rakic, 2002; Ardid et al., 2015; Rich and Wallis, 2017; Voloh and Womelsdorf, 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior primate literature.

claim: Narrow spiking putative interneurons show stronger encoding of feature-specific reward prediction errors compared to broad spiking neurons.
source: Compared to broad spiking neurons the group of narrow spiking, putative interneurons in lateral prefrontal cortex have been found to more likely encode categorical information during working memory delays (Diester and Nieder, 2008), show stronger stimulus onset responses during cognitive control tasks (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger attentional modulation (Thiele et al., 2016), more location-specific encoding of task rules (Johnston et al., 2009), stronger reduction of firing selectivity for task irrelevant stimulus features (Hussar and Pasternak, 2009), stronger encoding of errors and loss (Shen et al., 2015; Sajad et al., 2019), more likely encoding of outcome history (Kawai et al., 2019), and stronger encoding of feature-specific reward prediction errors (Oemisch et al., 2019), amongst other unique firing characteristics (Constantinidis and Goldman-Rakic, 2002; Ardid et al., 2015; Rich and Wallis, 2017; Voloh and Womelsdorf, 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior primate literature.

claim: >95% of all PV+ interneurons in prefrontal cortex show narrow spike width.
source: Comparisons of protein expression with action potential spike width have shown for prefrontal cortex that > 95% of all PV+ and ~ 87% of all SOM + interneurons show narrow spike width (Ghaderi et al., 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020), while narrow spikes are also known to occur in ~20% of VIP interneurons (Torres-Gomez et al., 2020) among other GABAergic neurons (Krimer et al., 2005; Zaitsev et al., 2009), and (at least in primate motor cortex) in a subgroup of pyramidal cells (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ~87% of all SOM+ interneurons in prefrontal cortex show narrow spike width.
source: Comparisons of protein expression with action potential spike width have shown for prefrontal cortex that > 95% of all PV+ and ~ 87% of all SOM + interneurons show narrow spike width (Ghaderi et al., 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020), while narrow spikes are also known to occur in ~20% of VIP interneurons (Torres-Gomez et al., 2020) among other GABAergic neurons (Krimer et al., 2005; Zaitsev et al., 2009), and (at least in primate motor cortex) in a subgroup of pyramidal cells (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Narrow spikes occur in ~20% of VIP interneurons.
source: Comparisons of protein expression with action potential spike width have shown for prefrontal cortex that > 95% of all PV+ and ~ 87% of all SOM + interneurons show narrow spike width (Ghaderi et al., 2018; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020), while narrow spikes are also known to occur in ~20% of VIP interneurons (Torres-Gomez et al., 2020) among other GABAergic neurons (Krimer et al., 2005; Zaitsev et al., 2009), and (at least in primate motor cortex) in a subgroup of pyramidal cells (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: At least three different types of firing patterns exist in narrow spiking neurons of monkeys during attention demanding tasks.
source: In addition, electrophysiological characterization has shown at least three different types of firing patterns in narrow spiking neurons of monkeys during attention demanding tasks (Ardid et al., 2015; Dasilva et al., 2019; Trainito et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior primate literature.

claim: 329 single neurons were recorded in LPFC areas 46/9 and anterior area 8.
source: During reversal performance, we recorded the activity of 329 single neurons in LPFC areas 46/9 and anterior area 8 (monkey H/K: 172/157) and 397 single neurons in dorsal ACC area 24 (monkey H/K: 213/184) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: 397 single neurons were recorded in dorsal ACC area 24.
source: During reversal performance, we recorded the activity of 329 single neurons in LPFC areas 46/9 and anterior area 8 (monkey H/K: 172/157) and 397 single neurons in dorsal ACC area 24 (monkey H/K: 213/184) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: The average action potential waveform shape of recorded neurons distinguished neurons with broad and narrow spikes.
source: The average action potential waveform shape of recorded neurons distinguished neurons with broad and narrow spikes similar to previous studies in LPFC and ACC (Gregoriou et al., 2012; Ardid et al., 2015; Westendorff et al., 2016; Dasilva et al., 2019; Oemisch et al., 2019; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: In LPFC 21% neurons had narrow spikes (n = 259 broad, n = 70 narrow cells).
source: We found in LPFC 21% neurons had narrow spikes (n = 259 broad, n = 70 narrow cells) and in ACC 17% of neurons had narrow action potentials (n = 331 broad, n = 66 narrow cells).
evidence: This is a direct report of the classification results from the data.

claim: In ACC 17% of neurons had narrow action potentials (n = 331 broad, n = 66 narrow cells).
source: We found in LPFC 21% neurons had narrow spikes (n = 259 broad, n = 70 narrow cells) and in ACC 17% of neurons had narrow action potentials (n = 331 broad, n = 66 narrow cells).
evidence: This is a direct report of the classification results from the data.

claim: B-type cells showed on average a symmetric pre- to post- spike triggered MUA activity modulation indicative of excitatory participation with local activity.
source: We found that B-type cells showed on average a symmetric pre- to post- spike triggered MUA activity modulation indicative of excitatory participation with local activity (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered MUA analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Spikes of N-type cells were followed by a faster drop of MUA activity indicating an inhibitory influence on MUA.
source: In contrast, spikes of N-type cells were followed by a faster drop of MUA activity indicating an inhibitory influence on MUA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered MUA analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The excitatory and inhibitory effects on local MUA activity significantly distinguished B- and N-type neurons (MUA modulation index for B- vs N-type cells, Wilcoxon test, p=0.001).
source: The excitatory and inhibitory effects on local MUA activity were consistent across the population and significantly distinguished B- and N-type neurons (Figure 1G; MUA modulation index: [(post MUAspike - pre MUAspike)/pre MUAspike] for B- vs N-type cells, Wilcoxon test, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike-triggered MUA data.

claim: The distinction between B- and N-type neurons based on MUA modulation was evident in ACC and in LPFC.
source: This distinction was evident in ACC and in LPFC (Figure 1H; for the N-type the MUA modulation index was different from zero, Wilcoxon test, in ACC, p<0.001, and in LPFC, p=0.03; for B-type cells the difference was not sign.).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Narrow spiking cells contain mostly inhibitory interneurons.
source: These findings suggest narrow spiking cells contain mostly inhibitory interneurons (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spike-triggered MUA analysis.

claim: Many neurons in LPFC selectively increased their firing to the color attention cue with no apparent modulation to the motion action cue (n = 71 cells).
source: Many neurons in LPFC selectively increased their firing to the color attention cue with no apparent modulation to the motion action cue (n = 71 cells with firing increases to the color but not motion cue) (for examples: Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of neuronal responses shown in Figure 2.

claim: N-type neurons in LPFC change transiently their firing to the attention cue when it occurred either early or late relative to the action cue (significant increase within 25–275 ms post-cue for Feature 1 and within 50–250 ms post-cue for Feature 2, p<0.05).
source: We found that N-type neurons in LPFC change transiently their firing to the attention cue when it occurred either early or late relative to the action cue (significant increase within 25–275 ms post-cue for Feature 1 and within 50–250 ms post-cue for Feature 2, p<0.05 randomization statistics, n = 21 N-type cells with increases and seven with decreases to the color cue, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: B-type neurons in LPFC did not show an attention cue-specific increase (n.s., randomization statistics).
source: This attention cue-specific increase was absent in B-type neurons in LPFC (n.s., randomization statistics, n = 44 B-type cells with increases and n = 35 with decreases to the color cue, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ACC N- and B-type neurons did not show an on-response to the color cue.
source: In contrast to LPFC, ACC N- and B-type neurons did not show an on-response to the color cue (n = 36/6 B- and N- type cells with increases, respectively, and n = 31/12 B- and N- type cells with decreased firing, respectively, to the color cue, the total cell number included in this analysis for the B- and N- type was n = 216/50, respectively) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The proportion of neurons whose firing rate significantly distinguished rewarded and nonrewarded colors sharply increased for N-type cells after the onset of the color cue in LPFC (18%; n = 10 of 54 N-type cells, randomization test p<0.05 within [175 575] ms after cue onset).
source: We found that the proportion of neurons whose firing rate significantly distinguished rewarded and nonrewarded colors sharply increased for N-type cells after the onset of the color cue in LPFC proportion of color selective responses within 0–0.5 s. after cue, 18%; n = 10 of 54 N-type cells, randomization test p<0.05 within [175 575] ms after cue onset, but not in ACC (cells with significant information: 6%; n = 3 of 50 N-type cells, ns., randomization test within [300 700] ms after cue onset) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: N-type cells in LPFC showed significant encoding of the right versus left location of the rewarded stimulus (22% with reward location information; n = 12 of 54 N-type cells, randomization test p<0.05 within [200 500] ms after cue onset).
source: Similar to the selectivity for the rewarded stimulus color N-type cells in LPFC (but not in ACC) showed significant encoding of the right versus left location of the rewarded stimulus (in LPFC: 22% with reward location information; n = 12 of 54 N-type cells, randomization test p<0.05 within [200 500] ms after cue onset; in ACC: 10% with reward location information; n = 5 of 50 N-type cells, n.s. randomization test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: During the post-color onset time period 17% (n = 20 of 120) of B-type cells and 27% (n = 11 of 41) of N-type cells in LPFC significantly correlated their firing with p(choice).
source: We found that during the post-color onset time period 17% (n = 20 of 120) of B-type cells and 27% (n = 11 of 41) of N-type cells in LPFC significantly correlated their firing with p(choice), which was larger than expected by chance (binomial test B-type cells: p<0.001; N-type cells: p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate correlations with choice probability.

claim: N-type cells in LPFC showed positive correlations with p(choice) (Pearson r = 0.068, Wilcoxon rank test, p=0.011).
source: On average, N-type cells in LPFC showed positive correlations (Pearson r = 0.068, Wilcoxon rank test, p=0.011), while B-type neurons showed on average no correlation (Wilcoxon rank test, p=0.20) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The positive p(choice) correlations of N-type neurons in LPFC grew following color onset and remained significant for 0.7 s following color onset (N = 41 N-type neurons, randomization test, p<0.05 from 0 to 0.7 s post-cue).
source: The positive p(choice) correlations of N-type neurons in LPFC grew following color onset and remained significant for 0.7 s following color onset (N = 41 N-type neurons, randomization test, p<0.05 from 0 to 0.7 s post-cue, Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Significantly less N-type cells in ACC correlated their firing with choice probability compared to LPFC (6%, n = 2 of 33 in ACC, versus 27% in LPFC, X2-test for prop. difference, X2-stat = 5.45, p=0.019).
source: Compared to LPFC, significantly less N-type cells in ACC correlated their firing with choice probability (6%, n = 2 of 33 in ACC, versus 27% in LPFC, X2-test for prop. difference, X2-stat = 5.45, p=0.019) and showed no p(choice) correlations over time (Wilcoxon rank test, p=0.49, n.s., Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison between ACC and LPFC shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In both LPFC and ACC, N- and B-type cells on average increased firing after the reward onset.
source: In both, LPFC and ACC, N- and B-type cells on average increased firing after the reward onset (p<0.05, randomization test, n = 26 of 54 and 18 of 188 B- type cells with increases, respectively, and n = 14 of 54 N- type and 5 of 188 B-type cells with decreased firing in LPFC, and n = 30 of 50 N-type and 13 of 216 B- type cells with increases, respectively, and n = 19 of 50 and 8 of 216 B-type cells with decreased firing in ACC).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of reward-evoked responses.

claim: The N- and B-type responses to the reward were not significantly different in ACC or LPFC.
source: However, the N- and B-type responses to the reward were not significantly different in ACC or LPFC (ns., randomization test, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: On average 23% of LPFC and 35% of ACC neurons showed significant firing rate correlations with RPE in the post-outcome epoch.
source: We found that on average 23% of LPFC and 35% of ACC neurons showed significant firing rate correlations with RPE in the post-outcome epoch with only moderately and non-significantly more N-type than B-type neurons having significant rate-RPE correlations (n = 9 N-type neurons, n = 31 B-type neurons, X2-test; p=0.64 for LPFC; n = 15 N-type neurons, n = 47 B-type neurons, X2-test; p=0.83 for ACC; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Time-resolved analysis revealed a significant positive firing x RPE correlation in the 0.2–0.6 s after reward onset for ACC N-type neurons, which was absent in LPFC (ACC, n = 43 N-type neurons, randomization test p<0.05; LPFC: n = 31 N-type neurons, no time bin with sign.).
source: However, time-resolved analysis of the strength of the average correlations revealed a significant positive firing x RPE correlation in the 0.2–0.6 s after reward onset for ACC N-type neurons, which was absent in LPFC (ACC, n = 43 N-type neurons, randomization test p<0.05; LPFC: n = 31 N-type neurons, no time bin with sign.; Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Clustering resulted in eight e-types.
source: We ran the k-means clustering algorithm on neurons in ACC and LPFC using variables mentioned above and their firing rate (details in Materials and methods). Clustering resulted in eight e-types (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Narrow spiking neurons fell into three e-types.
source: Narrow spiking neurons fell into three e-types. The first narrow spiking N1 e-type (n = 18, 13% of narrow spiking neurons) showed high firing rates and highly regular spike trains (low LVs, mean LV 0.47, SE 0.05). The second N2 e-type (n = 27, 20% of narrow spiking neurons) showed on average Poisson spike train variability (LVs around 1) and the narrowest waveforms, and the N3 e-type (n = 91, 67% of all narrow spiking neurons) showed intermediate narrow waveform duration and regular firing (LV's < 1, mean LV 0.84, SE 0.02) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The N1 e-type (n = 18, 13% of narrow spiking neurons) showed high firing rates and highly regular spike trains (low LVs, mean LV 0.47, SE 0.05).
source: The first narrow spiking N1 e-type (n = 18, 13% of narrow spiking neurons) showed high firing rates and highly regular spike trains (low LVs, mean LV 0.47, SE 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis results.

claim: The N2 e-type (n = 27, 20% of narrow spiking neurons) showed on average Poisson spike train variability (LVs around 1) and the narrowest waveforms.
source: The second N2 e-type (n = 27, 20% of narrow spiking neurons) showed on average Poisson spike train variability (LVs around 1) and the narrowest waveforms, and the N3 e-type (n = 91, 67% of all narrow spiking neurons) showed intermediate narrow waveform duration and regular firing (LV's < 1, mean LV 0.84, SE 0.02) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The N3 e-type (n = 91, 67% of all narrow spiking neurons) showed intermediate narrow waveform duration and regular firing (LV's < 1, mean LV 0.84, SE 0.02).
source: The second N2 e-type (n = 27, 20% of narrow spiking neurons) showed on average Poisson spike train variability (LVs around 1) and the narrowest waveforms, and the N3 e-type (n = 91, 67% of all narrow spiking neurons) showed intermediate narrow waveform duration and regular firing (LV's < 1, mean LV 0.84, SE 0.02) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neurons within an e-type showed similar feature characteristics irrespective of whether they were from ACC or LPFC.
source: Neurons within an e-type showed similar feature characteristics irrespective of whether they were from ACC or LPFC. For example, N3 e-type neurons from ACC and in LPFC were indistinguishable in their firing and action potential characteristics (LVACC / LPFC = 0.79/0.88, ranksum-test, p=0.06; CVACC / LPFC = 1.19/1.31, ranksum-test, p=0.07; Firing RateACC/LPFC = 4.41/4.29, ranksum-test p=0.71; action potential repolarization time (hyperpolarization rate)ACC / PFC = 0.18 sec. (97 s.−1)/0.17 s. (93 s.−1)).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of N3 e-type neurons across areas.

claim: Only the N3 e-type showed a spike-triggered MUA modulation ratio different from zero (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Across all e-types only the spike-triggered MUA modulation ratio for the N3 e-type was different from zero (p<0.05, FDR-corrected) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The spike-triggered MUA modulation ratio for the N3 e-type differed significantly from the B4 (p=0.02) and B5 (p=0.03) e-types.
source: Comparison between cell classes showed that the spike-triggered MUA modulation ratio for the N3 e-type differed significantly from the B4 (p=0.02) and B5 (p=0.03) e-types.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison between e-types.

claim: The only e-type with a significant average correlation of firing and choice probability during the cue period was the N3 e-type in LPFC (r = 0.08, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.04; randomization test difference to zero, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison corrected, p<0.05).
source: We found that the only e-type with a significant average correlation of firing and choice probability during the cue period was the N3 e-type in LPFC (r = 0.08, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.04; randomization test difference to zero, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison corrected, p<0.05; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Neurons of the N3 e-type in LPFC significantly increased firing to the color cue, irrespective of whether the color cue appeared early or later in the trial (p<0.05 during 0.04–0.2 s after feature two onset, and p<0.05 during 0.175–0.225 s after feature one onset).
source: Consistent with this correlation, neurons of the N3 e-type in LPFC also significantly increased firing to the color cue, irrespective of whether the color cue appeared early or later in the trial (p<0.05 during 0.04–0.2 s after feature two onset, and p<0.05 during 0.175–0.225 s after feature one onset, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In LPFC, a linear classifier trained on multiclass p(choice) values was able to label N3 e-type neurons based on their p(choice) values with an accuracy of 31%.
source: In LPFC, a linear classifier trained on multiclass p(choice) values was able to label N3 e-type neurons based on their p(choice) values with an accuracy of 31% (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning classification analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In ACC, the N3 e-type was the only narrow spiking subclass with a significant functional firing rate correlation with reward prediction errors (RPE) (n = 30 neurons; r = 0.09, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.01, randomization test for sign. difference to zero, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison corrected p<0.05).
source: Similar to the N3 e-type in LPFC, in ACC it was the N3 e-type that was the only narrow spiking subclass with a significant functional firing rate correlation with reward prediction errors (RPE) (n = 30 neurons; r = 0.09, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.01, randomization test for sign. difference to zero, Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison corrected p<0.05, Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The B4 class in ACC fired stronger with lower RPE's (n = 18 neurons; r = −0.08, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.01, randomization test for sign. difference to zero, multiple comparison corrected p<0.05).
source: The only other e-type with a significant firing rate x RPE correlation was the B4 class which fired stronger with lower RPE's (n = 18 neurons; r = −0.08, Kruskal Wallis test, p=0.01, randomization test for sign. difference to zero, multiple comparison corrected p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate correlations with RPE.

claim: In ACC, a linear classifier trained on multiclass RPE values was able to label N3 e-type neurons from their RPE value with an accuracy of 34%.
source: In ACC, a linear classifier trained on multiclass RPE values was able to label N3 e-type neurons from their RPE value with an accuracy of 34% (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning classification analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: STAs of many N3 e-type neurons showed oscillatory sidelobes in the 10–30 Hz range.
source: We first inspected the spike-triggered LFP averages (STAs) of neurons and found that STAs of many N3 e-type neurons showed oscillatory sidelobes in the 10–30 Hz range (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-triggered LFP analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The density of spike-LFP synchrony peaks showed a high prevalence of 15–30 Hz beta synchrony for broad spiking neurons in both ACC and LPFC.
source: The density of spike-LFP synchrony peaks, measured as the proportion of neurons that show reliable PPC peaks (see Materials and methods), showed a high prevalence of 15–30 Hz beta synchrony for broad spiking neurons in both, ACC and LPFC, a peak of ~5–12 Hz synchrony that was unique to ACC, and a high prevalence of 35–45 Hz gamma synchronization in narrow spiking cells (but not in broad spiking cells) in both areas (Figure 6C; Voloh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike-LFP synchrony shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a high prevalence of 35–45 Hz gamma synchronization in narrow spiking cells (but not in broad spiking cells) in both ACC and LPFC.
source: The density of spike-LFP synchrony peaks, measured as the proportion of neurons that show reliable PPC peaks (see Materials and methods), showed a high prevalence of 15–30 Hz beta synchrony for broad spiking neurons in both, ACC and LPFC, a peak of ~5–12 Hz synchrony that was unique to ACC, and a high prevalence of 35–45 Hz gamma synchronization in narrow spiking cells (but not in broad spiking cells) in both areas (Figure 6C; Voloh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spike-LFP synchrony shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In LPFC, the N3 e-type neurons showed a sharp increase in 35–45 Hz gamma band synchrony shortly after the color cue is presented when choice probabilities were low.
source: We found in LPFC that the N3 e-type neurons showed a sharp increase in 35–45 Hz gamma band synchrony shortly after the color cue is presented and choice probabilities were low (i.e. when the animals were uncertain which stimulus is rewarded), while broad spiking neurons did not show gamma synchrony (Figure 7A–C) (N3 e-type vs broad spiking cell difference in gamma synchrony in the 0–700 ms after color cue onset: p<0.05, randomization test, multiple comparison corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved spike-LFP synchrony analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: When choice probabilities are high, N3 e-type neurons and broad spiking neurons in LPFC showed significant increases of 20–35 Hz beta-band synchronization.
source: When choice probabilities are high, N3 e-type neurons and broad spiking neurons in LPFC showed significant increases of 20–35 Hz beta-band synchronization (Figure 7D,E) with N3 e-type neurons synchronizing significantly stronger to beta than broad spiking neuron types (Figure 7F) (p<0.05 randomization test, multiple comparison corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved spike-LFP synchrony analysis shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: In ACC, the N3 e-type neurons synchronized in a 35–42 Hz gamma band following the reward onset when RPE's were high.
source: In ACC, the N3 e-type neurons synchronized in a 35–42 Hz gamma band following the reward onset when RPE's were high (i.e. when outcomes were unexpected), which was weaker and emerged later when RPEs were low, and which was absent in broad spiking neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved spike-LFP synchrony analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: In ACC, low RPE trials triggered increased spike-LFP synchronization at a ~ 6–14 Hz theta/alpha frequency in the N3 e-type neurons.
source: In contrast to this gamma synchronization at high RPE, low RPE trials triggered increased spike-LFP synchronization at a ~ 6–14 Hz theta/alpha frequency in the N3 e-type neurons (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved spike-LFP synchrony analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The increase of 6–14 Hz synchrony in ACC was significantly stronger in the N3 e-type than in broad spiking neurons in the 0 to 0.7 s post reward onset period.
source: The increase of 6–14 Hz synchrony was significantly stronger in the N3 e-type than in broad spiking neurons in the 0 to 0.7 s post reward onset period (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The N3 e-type significantly stronger gamma synchronized in the reward period when RPEs were high (p=0.04, Tukey-Kramer, multiple comparison corrected).
source: Comparison to the other e-types showed that the N3 e-type significantly stronger gamma synchronized in the reward period when RPEs were high (p=0.04, Tukey-Kramer, multiple comparison corrected) (Figure 7—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The spike-LFP synchronization results in PFC and in ACC were unchanged when the average reward onset aligned LFP, or the average color-cue aligned LFP was subtracted prior to the analysis.
source: The spike-LFP synchronization results in PFC and in ACC were unchanged when the average reward onset aligned LFP, or the average color-cue aligned LFP was subtracted prior to the analysis, which controls for a possible influence of lower frequency evoked potentials (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The E-I network model can synchronize by way of mutual inhibition at beta or gamma frequencies depending on the total amount of drive the network receives.
source: Such an E-I network can synchronize by way of mutual inhibition at beta or gamma frequencies depending on the total amount of drive the network receives (Wang and Buzsáki, 1996; White et al., 1998; Tiesinga and José, 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on prior theoretical work cited in the manuscript.

claim: When both stimuli have similar values and the choice probability is relatively low, the drive to the network is high and it synchronizes in the gamma band.
source: When both stimuli have similar values and the choice probability is relatively low, the drive to the network is high and it synchronizes in the gamma band. In contrast, when one of the objects has a value that is much larger than the other which results in high choice probabilities for that stimulus, it results in a net level of drive that makes the network synchronize in the beta band.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model described in the manuscript.

claim: When one of the objects has a value that is much larger than the other which results in high choice probabilities for that stimulus, it results in a net level of drive that makes the network synchronize in the beta band.
source: When both stimuli have similar values and the choice probability is relatively low, the drive to the network is high and it synchronizes in the gamma band. In contrast, when one of the objects has a value that is much larger than the other which results in high choice probabilities for that stimulus, it results in a net level of drive that makes the network synchronize in the beta band.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model described in the manuscript.

claim: The N3 e-type in LPFC synchronized at gamma when p(choice) was relatively low and at beta frequencies otherwise.
source: The N3 e-type in LPFC synchronized at gamma when p(choice) was relatively low and at beta frequencies otherwise.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings shown in Figure 7 and Figure 9A.

claim: In ACC the N3 e-type synchronized at gamma when the prediction error was large and at theta frequencies otherwise.
source: In ACC the N3 e-type synchronized at gamma when the prediction error was large and at theta frequencies otherwise.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings shown in Figure 8 and Figure 9B.

claim: The N3 e-type neurons will be mostly PV+ cells.
source: With regard to the specific interneuron e-types we believe that the N3 e-type that showed functional correlations in two areas encompasses mostly parvalbumin PV+ expressing neurons, because of their narrow spikes, regular inter-spike intervals and their propensity to synchronize at gamma, which resemble the regular firing and gamma synchrony described for PV+ cells in the rodent (Cardin et al., 2009; Tiesinga, 2012; Stark et al., 2013; Amilhon et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Gouwens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparison with rodent literature.

claim: Similar to the N3 e-type responses to the attention cue, rodent dorsomedial frontal PV+ neurons systematically activate to preparatory cues while somatostatin neurons respond significantly less.
source: Moreover, similar to the N3 e-type responses to the attention cue, rodent dorsomedial frontal PV+ neurons systematically activate to preparatory cues while somatostatin neurons respond significantly less (Pinto and Dan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to rodent literature.

claim: PV+ neurons are heterogeneous and entail Chandelier cells and variably sized basket cells.
source: However, PV+ neurons are heterogeneous and entail Chandelier cells and variably sized basket cells (Markram et al., 2004; Markram et al., 2015; Gouwens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The N3 e-type was distinguished from other narrow spiking neurons by having a lower firing rate and an intermediate-narrow action potential shape as opposed to the narrowest waveform and highest firing rates that N1 e-types showed.
source: It might therefore be an important observation that the N3 e-type was distinguished from other narrow spiking neurons by having a lower firing rate and an intermediate-narrow action potential shape as opposed to the narrowest waveform and highest firing rates that N1 e-types showed.
evidence: This is an observation from the clustering analysis results.

claim: N3 e-type neurons would not be part of calretinin (CR+) or calbindin (CB+) expressing cells as their expression profiles do not apparently overlap with PV+.
source: The proposed tentative suggestion that N3 e-type neurons will be mostly PV+ cells also entails for the primate brain that they would not be part of calretinin (CR+) or calbindin (CB+) expressing cells as their expression profiles do not apparently overlap (Dombrowski et al., 2001; Medalla and Barbas, 2009; Raghanti et al., 2010; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about protein expression patterns.

claim: Assuming that N3 e-type neurons are partly PV+ neurons, this translates into gamma rhythmic inhibition of local circuit pyramidal cells close to their soma where they impose output gain control.
source: Assuming that N3 e-type neurons are partly PV+ neurons, we speculate that this translates into gamma rhythmic inhibition of local circuit pyramidal cells close to their soma where they impose output gain control (Tiesinga et al., 2004; Bartos et al., 2007; Womelsdorf et al., 2014b; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on cited literature about PV+ neuron function.

claim: The putative function of N3 e-type cells in LPFC is the gating of competing excitatory inputs.
source: We therefore speculate that the putative circuit function of the N3 e-type cells in LPFC is the gating of competing excitatory inputs (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the computational model and empirical data.

claim: The proposed circuit model for the ACC suggests that the N3 e-type neurons activate when there is a mismatch of reward and chosen value.
source: In summary, the proposed circuit model for the ACC suggests that the N3 e-type neurons activate when there is a mismatch of reward and chosen value. Activation of the N3 e-type neurons may thus be a (bio-) marker that predictions need to be updated to improve future performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the computational model and empirical data.

claim: Activation of the N3 e-type neurons may be a (bio-) marker that predictions need to be updated to improve future performance.
source: In summary, the proposed circuit model for the ACC suggests that the N3 e-type neurons activate when there is a mismatch of reward and chosen value. Activation of the N3 e-type neurons may thus be a (bio-) marker that predictions need to be updated to improve future performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the computational model and empirical data.

claim: Narrow spiking interneurons are the main carriers of gamma rhythmic activity in nonhuman primate prefrontal cortex during cue and outcomes processing.
source: Our findings provide strong empirical evidence that narrow spiking interneurons are the main carriers of gamma rhythmic activity in nonhuman primate prefrontal cortex during cue and outcomes processing (Whittington et al., 2000; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Bartos et al., 2007; Hasenstaub et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Shin and Moore, 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the empirical findings and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gamma activity of N3 e-type neurons indexes a key function of LPFC and ACC.
source: Considering this ACC finding together with the LPFC finding suggests that gamma activity of N3 e-type neurons indexes a key function of these brain areas, supporting recent causal evidence from rodent optogenetics (Cho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the empirical findings and supported by a citation to rodent optogenetics.

claim: Blocking inhibition with GABA antagonists like bicuculline renders fast spiking interneurons nonselective during working memory tasks and abolishes the spatial tuning of regular spiking (excitatory) cells during working memory tasks in monkeys.
source: Blocking inhibition with GABA antagonists like bicuculline not only renders fast spiking interneurons nonselective during working memory tasks but abolishes the spatial tuning of regular spiking (excitatory) cells during working memory tasks in monkeys (Sawaguchi et al., 1989; Rao et al., 2000), disturbs accuracy in attention tasks (Paine et al., 2011) and reduces set shifting flexibility by enhancing perseveration (Enomoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Abnormally enhancing GABAa levels via muscimol impairs working memory and set shifting behavior.
source: Similarly, abnormally enhancing GABAa levels via muscimol impairs working memory and set shifting behavior (Rich and Shapiro, 2007; Urban et al., 2014) and can result in either maladaptive impulsive behaviors (Paine et al., 2015), and when applied in anterior cingulate cortex to perseveration (Amiez et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Altered medial and lateral prefrontal cortex inhibition is closely linked to an inability to adjust attentional strategies given unexpected outcomes.
source: Thus, altered medial and lateral prefrontal cortex inhibition is closely linked to an inability to adjust attentional strategies given unexpected outcomes. This evidence supports our studies suggestion of the importance of inhibitory neuron involvement in resolving uncertainties during adaptive behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental literature.
